source.title: A Toy Model of Universality: Reverse Engineering How Networks Learn Group Operations
source.authors: Bilal Chughtai; Lawrence Chan; Neel Nanda

record.tranche_reason: Tests grokking and its gradual internal progress measures on group-composition models, using a representation-theoretic analysis rather than the original modular-addition Fourier analysis.
record.gate_note: The paper reports grokking on S5 and studies progress measures, weight norms, and learned circuits. It cites results from other work, which are not recorded as rows. The training-set fraction is stated, but the paper does not vary training-set size.
record.test_reason: The study reproduces grokking on S5 composition, the same group task Power et al. used. It applies Nanda-style restricted and excluded progress measures to a new representation-theoretic circuit. It also tests whether the algorithm is shared across seeds, groups and architectures. Its own results bear on V1, V2, V5 and V6. It is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is correct. Small networks learn group composition via a representation-theoretic (GCR) algorithm across groups and architectures. The specific representations, their number and their order vary, which is evidence for weak but not strong universality. Progress measures show memorization, then circuit formation, then cleanup, with grokking during cleanup. The authors also link grokking to weight norm and weight decay.
record.recipe_differences: Adapts the mechanistic progress-measure approach used for modular addition to finite-group composition, using representation matrices and character theory rather than focusing on Fourier modes. Uses S5 as the mainline task and also studies other groups and architectures.
record.method_sensitivity: The learned representations and their order vary with random seed and architecture; the paper also reports that different groups and hyperparameters yield different representation choices.
record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 202, 2023
record.problems: The main grokking accuracy plot is not numerically tabulated in the text. The study uses one training-data fraction for its mainline setup and does not test whether smaller training sets increase the delay. Results across groups and architectures in Table 3 are averages over 4 seeds, with no uncertainty estimates stated.

untested.parts: Whether the delay grows as the training set shrinks; only a 40% training fraction is used.
Critical dataset size and ungrokking below it; no sweep of weight-decay strength.
Not tested: no non-algorithmic data and no sweep of initialization scale or weight norm.
Not tested: no large models trained on realistic data.
Not tested: no optimizer or numerical-precision controls.

missing.what: Test, excluded and restricted loss per group and architecture. Examples: MLP S5 test 1.02e-05, excluded 11.72, restricted 2.21e-07; Transformer C118 restricted 2.55e-01.
The network prefers the standard representation over standard-sign despite standard-sign's better performance at fixed weight norm.
Grokking also occurs under dropout instead of weight decay, and progress measures still apply.
A run with two successive grokking phases as the 5d_b representation is learned around epoch 100k.
Hidden sizes 32–256: smaller nets often fail to generalize. Those that generalize use GCR, with no size effect on which representations are learned.
Ablations on the mainline model. Excluding the standard-representation logit predictions raises loss to 7.23; restricting to them lowers loss by 70%.

record.verdict_notes: Tranche is borderline T1/T2: S5 composition matches Power et al.'s task, but the analysis method is new. Several Transformer runs have non-trivial restricted loss: C118 seed 4 at 1.01, D61 seed 2 at 0.38, A5 seed 3 with test loss 0.195. The algorithm therefore does not fully account for performance in every run. No uncertainty estimates are reported; Table 3 values are means over 4 seeds.

versions.untested_parts: The paper tests for grokking on group-composition tasks, but does not vary training-set size or test whether smaller sets cause longer delays.
Tests gradual circuit formation and later cleanup using restricted and excluded loss; does not test every possible progress measure or generalizing algorithm.
No non-algorithmic data or initialization-scale/weight-norm sweep to switch grokking on or off.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic data.
Reports evidence linking weight decay, circuit formation/cleanup, and relative circuit weight. Does not test a critical dataset size, ungrokking below it, or alternative low-norm mechanisms.
Tests group-composition models across groups, architectures, and seeds. Does not test realistic tasks or establish a single identical set of features and circuits across all runs.
No controlled test of adaptive-optimizer instabilities or floating-point/softmax artifacts.

relation.reason: Reports its own grokking trajectories, circuit-development measurements, ablations, and comparisons across seeds and architectures.

tranche.reason: Tests grokking mechanisms with representation-theoretic circuit analysis and adapted restricted/excluded losses, extending the earlier Fourier-based method.

source_check.notes: The observed states for r8,r9 rely on joint circuit and ablation evidence; their FVE values alone do not establish algorithm identity, and Table 3 loss columns should be recorded. The study does not establish training-set-size dependence, a quantitative timing forecast, critical dataset size, or ungrokking; its weight-decay explanation is an attribution from the observed dynamics.
